Finally, in the toy setting we observe a two-phase learning dynamic: networks first memorize individual factual associations in a few steps, then -- over a longer horizon -- learn to linearly separate true from false, which in turn lowers language-modeling loss. Together, these results provide both a mechanistic demonstration and an empirical motivation for how and why linear truth representations can emerge in language models.

papers.title: Exploring Concept Depth: How Large Language Models Acquire Knowledge and Concept at Different Layers?
papers.research_question: Can shallow layers in LLMs capture meaningful features of simple knowledge, while complex concepts need deeper layers to capture their meaningful features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of 'Concept Depth' to measure how different layers in LLMs capture concepts of varying complexity, showing that simpler concepts are learned in shallow layers while complex concepts require deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: The Concept Depth metric provides a useful framework for understanding how LLMs process concepts of varying complexity across layers, and the experimental insights enhance the understanding of internal representations in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Simpler concepts (e.g., factual knowledge) are learned in shallow layers, while more complex concepts (e.g., reasoning tasks) require deeper layers for accurate understanding.
The pattern of Concept Depth is consistent across different model families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) and model sizes.
Larger models within a family tend to achieve higher peak accuracy and sometimes converge to optimal performance at earlier layers.
Adding noise to the input or quantizing model weights (e.g., to 8-bit) slows down the convergence of concept understanding, requiring deeper layers to achieve comparable accuracy.
Compressing models to 16-bit quantization does not significantly harm the understanding process compared to 32-bit.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performances across a wide range of tasks. However, the mechanisms by which these models encode tasks of varying complexities remain poorly understood. In this paper, we explore the hypothesis that LLMs process concepts of varying complexities in different layers, introducing the idea of "Concept Depth" to suggest that more complex concepts are typically acquired in deeper layers. Specifically, we categorize concepts based on their level of abstraction, defining them in the order of increasing complexity within factual, emotional, and inferential tasks. We conduct extensive probing experiments using layer-wise representations across various LLM families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) on various datasets spanning the three domains of tasks. Our findings reveal that models could efficiently conduct probing for simpler tasks in shallow layers, and more complex tasks typically necessitate deeper layers for accurate understanding. Additionally, we examine how external factors, such as adding noise to the input and quantizing the model weights, might affect layer-wise representations. Our findings suggest that these factors can impede the development of a conceptual understanding of LLMs until deeper layers are explored. We hope that our proposed concept and experimental insights will enhance the understanding of the mechanisms underlying LLMs. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Luckfort/CD.

papers.title: Where Knowledge Collides: A Mechanistic Study of Intra-Memory Knowledge Conflict in Language Models
papers.research_question: Which internal components of language models are responsible for encoding conflicting knowledge from pre-training data, and can noisy or incorrect information be selectively suppressed during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a mechanistic interpretability framework to localize and intervene on conflicting knowledge encoded in language models, showing that attention components in later layers play a key role in encoding and resolving such conflicts.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a mechanistic interpretability framework to study intra-memory knowledge conflict, demonstrating that logit inspection, activation patching, and cross-model patching can localize and intervene on conflicting internal representations at inference time.
papers.key_findings:
Conflicting training data reduces model confidence and introduces confusion in later layers.
Attention components in later layers dominate in shaping factual responses and encoding conflicting knowledge.
Activation patching can steer model generation toward accurate outputs, with success rates varying across models (up to 22% for GPT-2 XL and 70% for Qwen3-4B).
Cross-model activation patching (CMAP) improves steering success and reduces noise compared to standard activation patching, especially for certain conflict attributes.
Findings generalize across different model architectures (GPT-2 XL and Qwen3-4B), though intervention effectiveness varies.
papers.limitation:
Limited set of conflict types and restriction to a 1:1 ratio of conflicting information per entity.
Results are presented on a limited set of model architectures (GPT-2 XL and Qwen3-4B).
The underlying factors that drive the model's preference for one conflicting fact over another are not analyzed.
future_direction: Extend these methods to knowledge editing and robust information tracing across prompts and model variants.
Include more conflict types and multiple conflicting information per entity.
Evaluate across additional model families.
papers.abstract: In language models (LMs), intra-memory knowledge conflict largely arises when inconsistent information about the same event is encoded within the model's parametric knowledge. While prior work has primarily focused on resolving conflicts between a model's internal knowledge and external resources through approaches such as fine-tuning or knowledge editing, the problem of localizing conflicts that originate during pre-training within the model's internal representations remain unexplored. In this work, we design a framework based on mechanistic interpretability methods to identify where and how conflicting knowledge from the pre-training data is encoded within LMs. Our findings contribute to a growing body of evidence that specific internal components of a language model are responsible for encoding conflicting knowledge from pre-training, and we demonstrate how mechanistic interpretability methods can be leveraged to causally intervene in and control conflicting knowledge at inference time.

papers.title: The Queen of England is not England's Queen: On the Lack of Factual Coherency in PLMs
papers.research_question: What is the coherency of factual knowledge in Pre-trained Language Models, and how does it vary with different prompts and evidence?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the concept of coherency for factual knowledge in PLMs, demonstrates that PLMs have low coherency, and finds that including evidence paragraphs substantially improves coherency.
papers.conclusion: PLMs have poor coherency in factual knowledge, but evidence paragraphs help. Future work should focus on architectural, data, and interface improvements.
papers.key_findings:
PLMs have low coherency in factual knowledge.
Autoregressive PLMs perform worse than masked PLMs.
Optimized prompts do not improve coherency.
Including evidence paragraphs substantially improves coherency.
Coherency varies significantly with paraphrased prompts.
papers.limitation: For N-1 or N-M relations, it is difficult to exclude every possible answer, and only answers present in LAMA are excluded, which might negatively affect the results.
future_direction: Improve PLMs on architectural level.
Improve PLMs on data level.
Improve pre-training objectives and interface.
papers.abstract: Factual knowledge encoded in Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) enriches their representations and justifies their use as knowledge bases. Previous work has focused on probing PLMs for factual knowledge by measuring how often they can correctly predict an object entity given a subject and a relation, and improving fact retrieval by optimizing the prompts used for querying PLMs. In this work, we consider a complementary aspect, namely the coherency of factual knowledge in PLMs, i.e., how often can PLMs predict the subject entity given its initial prediction of the object entity. This goes beyond evaluating how much PLMs know, and focuses on the internal state of knowledge inside them. Our results indicate that PLMs have low coherency using manually written, optimized and paraphrased prompts, but including an evidence paragraph leads to substantial improvement. This shows that PLMs fail to model inverse relations and need further enhancements to be able to handle retrieving facts from their parameters in a coherent manner, and to be considered as knowledge bases.

papers.title: Calibrating Reasoning in Language Models with Internal Consistency
papers.research_question: How can internal representations in large language models be used to calibrate reasoning, specifically by measuring inconsistencies between intermediate and final layers during chain-of-thought reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes internal consistency as a novel measure to evaluate LLM confidence in reasoning by examining agreement of latent predictions from intermediate layers, and shows that up-weighting paths with high internal consistency significantly boosts reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: Internal consistency is a robust indicator of correct reasoning paths and can be leveraged to enhance the reliability of reasoning in LLMs through calibration.
papers.key_findings:
CoT reasoning leads to inconsistencies between middle and final layer representations, indicating uncertainty.
Internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths.
Up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency improves reasoning accuracy across various tasks.
Patterns in attention and feed-forward networks across layers provide insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency.
Layer-weighted aggregation of internal consistency finds transferable patterns that generalize across tasks.
papers.limitation:
The study is restricted to decoder-only models.
The analysis focuses on vanilla chain-of-thought prompting, not other complex prompting techniques.
future_direction: Extending the concept of internal consistency to encoder-decoder models.
Investigating internal consistency under more complex prompting scenarios.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in various reasoning tasks, aided by techniques like chain-of-thought prompting that elicits verbalized reasoning. However, LLMs often generate text with obvious mistakes and contradictions, raising doubts about their ability to robustly process and utilize generated rationales. In this work, we investigate reasoning in LLMs through the lens of internal representations, focusing on how these representations are influenced by generated rationales. Our preliminary analysis reveals that while generated rationales improve answer accuracy, inconsistencies emerge between the model's internal representations in middle layers and those in final layers, potentially undermining the reliability of their reasoning processes. To address this, we propose internal consistency as a measure of the model's confidence by examining the agreement of latent predictions decoded from intermediate layers. Extensive empirical studies across different models and datasets demonstrate that internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths. Motivated by this, we propose a new approach to calibrate reasoning by up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency, resulting in a significant boost in reasoning performance. Further analysis uncovers distinct patterns in attention and feed-forward modules across layers, providing insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency. In summary, our results demonstrate the potential of using internal representations for self-evaluation of LLMs. Our code is available at github.com/zhxieml/internal-consistency.

papers.title: Summing Up the Facts: Additive Mechanisms Behind Factual Recall in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do transformer-based large language models (LLMs) store and retrieve factual knowledge? The paper investigates the mechanistic story behind factual recall, focusing on prompts of the form 'Fact: The Colosseum is in the country of ____.'
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that factual recall in LLMs is achieved through an additive combination of multiple independent mechanisms (subject heads, relation heads, mixed heads, MLPs), termed the 'additive motif', and extends direct logit attribution to attribute attention head outputs to individual source tokens.
papers.conclusion: Factual recall in LLMs is achieved through additive combination of multiple independent mechanisms, and this additive motif may be a general principle in how models compute.
papers.key_findings:
There are four distinct mechanisms (subject heads, relation heads, mixed heads, MLPs) that additively combine to produce factual recall.
Each mechanism independently contributes to the correct logit, and their sum results in constructive interference, even if individual mechanisms are insufficient alone.
The additive motif explains why models often produce incorrect attributes alongside correct ones.
Extending direct logit attribution to attribute head outputs to source tokens reveals mixed heads as two separate additive updates from subject and relation tokens.
The work highlights a limitation of narrow circuit analysis that ignores multiple sources of information in prompts.
papers.limitation:
The dataset is small and hand-written, which may limit generalizability.
The analysis is limited to a specific prompting format and may not generalize to other tasks.
future_direction: Understanding correlation and superposition in feature representations
Understanding MLP neurons in detail
Studying how different prompting setups affect factual recall mechanisms
papers.abstract: How do transformer-based large language models (LLMs) store and retrieve knowledge? We focus on the most basic form of this task -- factual recall, where the model is tasked with explicitly surfacing stored facts in prompts of form `Fact: The Colosseum is in the country of'. We find that the mechanistic story behind factual recall is more complex than previously thought. It comprises several distinct, independent, and qualitatively different mechanisms that additively combine, constructively interfering on the correct attribute. We term this generic phenomena the additive motif: models compute through summing up multiple independent contributions. Each mechanism's contribution may be insufficient alone, but summing results in constructive interfere on the correct answer. In addition, we extend the method of direct logit attribution to attribute an attention head's output to individual source tokens. We use this technique to unpack what we call `mixed heads' -- which are themselves a pair of two separate additive updates from different source tokens.

papers.title: Knowledge Localization: Mission Not Accomplished? Enter Query Localization!
papers.research_question: Does the Knowledge Localization (KL) assumption hold for all facts? If not, what is a more realistic assumption?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Query Localization (QL) assumption, which includes query-KN mapping and dynamic KN selection, and introduces a Consistency-Aware KN modification method that improves knowledge editing performance.
papers.conclusion: The Query Localization assumption provides a more realistic framework for understanding knowledge storage and expression in LLMs than the Knowledge Localization assumption, and is validated by improved editing performance.
papers.key_findings:
Inconsistent Knowledge (KI) that violates the Knowledge Localization assumption is widespread in LLMs.
For KI, knowledge neurons are associated with specific queries rather than the fact itself (query-KN mapping).
The attention module plays a key role in selecting appropriate knowledge neurons for expression (dynamic KN selection).
The proposed Consistency-Aware KN modification method, based on the QL assumption, improves knowledge editing performance over baseline methods.
papers.limitation:
The work primarily focuses on factual knowledge, and it remains unclear whether the QL assumption applies to other types of knowledge.
The distinction between Consistent Knowledge (KC) and Inconsistent Knowledge (KI) might be related to the pre-training process.
future_direction: Exploring how to reconcile the QL assumption with other current theories.
Further utilizing the QL assumption to improve model editing methods.
Integrating the attention module more effectively to develop enhanced methods for dynamically editing knowledge.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) store extensive factual knowledge, but the mechanisms behind how they store and express this knowledge remain unclear. The Knowledge Neuron (KN) thesis is a prominent theory for explaining these mechanisms. This theory is based on the Knowledge Localization (KL) assumption, which suggests that a fact can be localized to a few knowledge storage units, namely knowledge neurons. However, this assumption has two limitations: first, it may be too rigid regarding knowledge storage, and second, it neglects the role of the attention module in knowledge expression. In this paper, we first re-examine the KL assumption and demonstrate that its limitations do indeed exist. To address these, we then present two new findings, each targeting one of the limitations: one focusing on knowledge storage and the other on knowledge expression. We summarize these findings as \textbf{Query Localization} (QL) assumption and argue that the KL assumption can be viewed as a simplification of the QL assumption. Based on QL assumption, we further propose the Consistency-Aware KN modification method, which improves the performance of knowledge modification, further validating our new assumption. We conduct 39 sets of experiments, along with additional visualization experiments, to rigorously confirm our conclusions. Code is available at https://github.com/heng840/KnowledgeLocalization.

papers.title: Probing the Geometry of Truth: Consistency and Generalization of Truth Directions in LLMs Across Logical Transformations and Question Answering Tasks
papers.research_question: Do LLMs universally represent truthfulness as a linear feature (truth direction)? Are simple probing techniques sufficiently expressive to identify truth directions? How does the truth direction generalize across logical transformations and question answering tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Consistent truth directions only emerge in capable LLMs and can be identified with simple linear probes; these probes generalize effectively to logical transformations, question answering, in-context learning, and external knowledge sources.
papers.conclusion: Truth directions are present in capable LLMs, can be identified with simple probes, and generalize well, highlighting their potential for eliciting latent knowledge and improving trust in LLM outputs.
papers.key_findings:
Not all LLMs exhibit consistent truth directions; this property is correlated with model capability, with stronger representations in more capable models.
Simple probes (linear SVM, logistic regression, MLP, mass-mean) are sufficient to identify truth directions when they exist.
Truthfulness probes generalize across logical negation, conjunction, and disjunction.
Truthfulness probes trained on atomic statements generalize to question answering tasks (MMLU, TriviaQA) and contextual knowledge tasks (SciQ, BoolQ, XSum).
Truthfulness probes can be used for selective question answering to filter out false answers, improving answer quality.
papers.limitation:
The term 'truth' may not be exactly what the probes measure; they likely capture an overlap between widely accepted human beliefs and objective truths.
Generalization is only tested on short-form QA; long-form QA and instruction-following tasks are not studied.
The causality of truthfulness probes is unclear; they may capture spuriously-correlated features rather than the target feature.
Computational resources limited evaluation to models up to Llama-3.1-70B, leaving more advanced models like GPT-4 untested.
future_direction: Extend analysis to more complex scenarios such as long-form QA and instruction-following tasks.
Study the causal implications of truth directions to guide LLMs toward more truthful responses.
Test the hypothesis on more advanced models like GPT-4.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are trained on extensive datasets that encapsulate substantial world knowledge. However, their outputs often include confidently stated inaccuracies. Earlier works suggest that LLMs encode truthfulness as a distinct linear feature, termed the "truth direction", which can classify truthfulness reliably. We address several open questions about the truth direction: (i) whether LLMs universally exhibit consistent truth directions; (ii) whether sophisticated probing techniques are necessary to identify truth directions; and (iii) how the truth direction generalizes across diverse contexts. Our findings reveal that not all LLMs exhibit consistent truth directions, with stronger representations observed in more capable models, particularly in the context of logical negation. Additionally, we demonstrate that truthfulness probes trained on declarative atomic statements can generalize effectively to logical transformations, question-answering tasks, in-context learning, and external knowledge sources. Finally, we explore the practical application of truthfulness probes in selective question-answering, illustrating their potential to improve user trust in LLM outputs. These results advance our understanding of truth directions and provide new insights into the internal representations of LLM beliefs. Our code is public at https://github.com/colored-dye/truthfulness_probe_generalization

papers.title: LLMs Know More Than They Show: On the Intrinsic Representation of LLM Hallucinations
papers.research_question: How much information about truthfulness is encoded in LLMs' internal representations, and how can it be used for error detection and analysis?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode truthfulness information in exact answer tokens, enabling improved error detection and analysis of error types, and revealing that truthfulness encoding is skill-specific rather than universal.
papers.conclusion: Internal representations of LLMs encode rich information about truthfulness and error types, which can guide error analysis and mitigation strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Truthfulness information is concentrated in exact answer tokens, and leveraging this improves error detection performance.
Error detectors based on probing do not generalize across tasks, indicating that truthfulness encoding is skill-specific.
Internal representations can predict error types (e.g., consistently incorrect, many answers).
There is a discrepancy between internal encoding and external behavior: the model may encode the correct answer but generate an incorrect one.
papers.limitation:
Error detectors do not generalize across datasets.
The error taxonomy is non-orthogonal, with overlapping categories.
future_direction: Further investigation is required to disentangle the multiple mechanisms of truthfulness encoding.
Potential directions for improvements in error analysis and mitigation using the model-centric framework.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often produce errors, including factual inaccuracies, biases, and reasoning failures, collectively referred to as "hallucinations". Recent studies have demonstrated that LLMs' internal states encode information regarding the truthfulness of their outputs, and that this information can be utilized to detect errors. In this work, we show that the internal representations of LLMs encode much more information about truthfulness than previously recognized. We first discover that the truthfulness information is concentrated in specific tokens, and leveraging this property significantly enhances error detection performance. Yet, we show that such error detectors fail to generalize across datasets, implying that -- contrary to prior claims -- truthfulness encoding is not universal but rather multifaceted. Next, we show that internal representations can also be used for predicting the types of errors the model is likely to make, facilitating the development of tailored mitigation strategies. Lastly, we reveal a discrepancy between LLMs' internal encoding and external behavior: they may encode the correct answer, yet consistently generate an incorrect one. Taken together, these insights deepen our understanding of LLM errors from the model's internal perspective, which can guide future research on enhancing error analysis and mitigation.

papers.title: Learning to Trust Your Feelings: Leveraging Self-awareness in LLMs for Hallucination Mitigation
papers.research_question: How well can LLMs discern and express their internal knowledge state to mitigate factual hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that LLMs can discern their internal knowledge state with high accuracy but often fail to express it, leading to hallucinations. It introduces the RLKF training framework, which uses knowledge feedback via reinforcement learning to improve model factuality and honesty.
papers.conclusion: RLKF is effective in improving the model's utilization of its internal knowledge state, enhancing performance in knowledge and honesty related tasks, and is a promising solution for hallucination mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs are highly adept at discerning their internal knowledge, with over 85% accuracy in knowledge probing.
DreamCatcher, an automatic hallucination detection tool, achieves 81% agreement with human annotators.
RLKF training enhances the factuality and honesty of LLMs, improving performance on knowledge-based tasks.
RLKF avoids the 'alignment tax' and improves benchmark performance on various tasks.
The reward model can quickly achieve high accuracy by utilizing internal knowledge state.
papers.abstract: We evaluate the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to discern and express their internal knowledge state, a key factor in countering factual hallucination and ensuring reliable application of LLMs. We observe a robust self-awareness of internal knowledge state in LLMs, evidenced by over 85% accuracy in knowledge probing. However, LLMs often fail to express their internal knowledge during generation, leading to factual hallucinations. We develop an automated hallucination annotation tool, Dreamcatcher, which merges knowledge probing and consistency checking methods to rank factual preference data. Using knowledge preference as reward, We propose a Reinforcement Learning from Knowledge Feedback (RLKF) training framework, leveraging reinforcement learning to enhance the factuality and honesty of LLMs. Our experiments across multiple models show that RLKF training effectively enhances the ability of models to utilize their internal knowledge state, boosting performance in a variety of knowledge-based and honesty-related tasks.

papers.title: Attention Satisfies: A Constraint-Satisfaction Lens on Factual Errors of Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) internally behave when they generate factually incorrect text, and can attention to constraint tokens predict factual errors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds a strong positive relationship between an LLM's attention to constraint tokens and the factual accuracy of its generations. It proposes SAT Probe, a method that probes attention patterns to predict factual errors and constraint satisfaction.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that attention patterns in LLMs provide a reliable signal for predicting factual errors, contributing to the mechanistic understanding of LLMs and offering a pathway to enhance their reliability.
papers.key_findings:
Attention to constraint tokens strongly correlates with the factual correctness of LLM generations.
SAT Probe, a linear probe on attention weights, can predict factual errors comparably to the model's own confidence score.
Larger LLMs tend to pay more attention to constraint tokens and achieve higher factual accuracy.
The total attention contribution from constraints across layers can be used to predict LLM success on factual queries.
Attention patterns can be used for early error identification, potentially stopping costly generation early.
papers.limitation: Exact match is used as a strict verification criterion for single-constraint queries, which could introduce noise to evaluations.
papers.abstract: We investigate the internal behavior of Transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) when they generate factually incorrect text. We propose modeling factual queries as constraint satisfaction problems and use this framework to investigate how the LLM interacts internally with factual constraints. We find a strong positive relationship between the LLM's attention to constraint tokens and the factual accuracy of generations. We curate a suite of 10 datasets containing over 40,000 prompts to study the task of predicting factual errors with the Llama-2 family across all scales (7B, 13B, 70B). We propose SAT Probe, a method probing attention patterns, that can predict factual errors and fine-grained constraint satisfaction, and allow early error identification. The approach and findings take another step towards using the mechanistic understanding of LLMs to enhance their reliability.

papers.title: Mass-Editing Memory in a Transformer
papers.research_question: How many memories can we add to a deep network by directly editing its weights? The paper investigates scaling up memory editing to thousands of associations in language models.
papers.core_contribution: MEMIT is a method for directly updating a language model with many memories by editing MLP weights in a range of critical layers, scaling to thousands of associations while maintaining generalization, specificity, and fluency.
papers.conclusion: MEMIT enables large-scale memory editing in transformers, and interpretability-based methods may become a practical alternative to opaque fine-tuning for editing, controlling, and auditing models.
papers.key_findings:
MEMIT scales to 10,000 edits on GPT-J and GPT-NeoX, exceeding prior work by orders of magnitude.
MEMIT outperforms fine-tuning, MEND, and ROME baselines on efficacy, generalization, and specificity metrics.
MEMIT maintains fluency and consistency of generations after mass edits.
MEMIT performs well across different categories of facts and when editing mixed sets of memories.
Certain relations (e.g., 'plays sport') are harder to edit with robust specificity, but MEMIT still outperforms other methods.
papers.limitation: The method is limited to directional (subject, relation, object) associations and does not cover symmetric relations, spatial/temporal reasoning, mathematical knowledge, or procedural knowledge.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown exciting promise in updating large language models with new memories, so as to replace obsolete information or add specialized knowledge. However, this line of work is predominantly limited to updating single associations. We develop MEMIT, a method for directly updating a language model with many memories, demonstrating experimentally that it can scale up to thousands of associations for GPT-J (6B) and GPT-NeoX (20B), exceeding prior work by orders of magnitude. Our code and data are at https://memit.baulab.info.

papers.title: DoLa: Decoding by Contrasting Layers Improves Factuality in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we reduce hallucinations in large language models by contrasting the logits from later versus earlier layers to better surface factual knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes DoLa, a decoding strategy that contrasts the logits from later versus earlier layers to amplify factual knowledge and reduce hallucinations in LLMs, without requiring external knowledge or fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: DoLa is an effective decoding strategy that improves factuality in LLMs across various tasks and model sizes, with minimal computational overhead.
papers.key_findings:
DoLa improves truthfulness on TruthfulQA by 12-17% absolute points across LLaMA models.
DoLa improves factuality on FACTOR, a long-paragraph factuality benchmark.
DoLa improves performance on chain-of-thought reasoning tasks (StrategyQA and GSM8K).
DoLa generates more factual and informative responses in open-ended chatbot evaluation (Vicuna QA) as rated by GPT-4.
DoLa introduces only a small latency overhead (1.01-1.08x) during decoding.
papers.limitation:
DoLa may not work well for small language models (e.g., GPT2) due to limited capacity and lack of distinct layer representations.
DoLa sometimes generates detailed factual information that may be less relevant to the question, indicating a trade-off between factuality and instruction following.
future_direction: Applying DoLa to other model families and tasks.
Exploring integration with instruction tuning.
Improving the ability to follow instructions while maintaining factuality.
papers.abstract: Despite their impressive capabilities, large language models (LLMs) are prone to hallucinations, i.e., generating content that deviates from facts seen during pretraining. We propose a simple decoding strategy for reducing hallucinations with pretrained LLMs that does not require conditioning on retrieved external knowledge nor additional fine-tuning. Our approach obtains the next-token distribution by contrasting the differences in logits obtained from projecting the later layers versus earlier layers to the vocabulary space, exploiting the fact that factual knowledge in an LLMs has generally been shown to be localized to particular transformer layers. We find that this Decoding by Contrasting Layers (DoLa) approach is able to better surface factual knowledge and reduce the generation of incorrect facts. DoLa consistently improves the truthfulness across multiple choices tasks and open-ended generation tasks, for example improving the performance of LLaMA family models on TruthfulQA by 12-17% absolute points, demonstrating its potential in making LLMs reliably generate truthful facts.

papers.title: Layer of Truth: Probing Belief Shifts under Continual Pre-Training Poisoning
papers.research_question: How does repeated exposure to plausible falsehoods during continual pre-training alter the internal factual representations (beliefs) in large language models? Specifically, does poisoning cause systematic belief replacement, where in the network is corruption localized and recoverable, and how do these shifts generalize across prompts, tasks, and languages?
papers.core_contribution: Continual pre-training on plausible misinformation can systematically overwrite specific factual knowledge in LLMs without degrading overall performance, with belief shifts concentrated in late transformer layers and generalizing across prompts and tasks.
papers.conclusion: Continual pre-training poisoning can overwrite internal factual representations without triggering broad performance collapse, motivating the need for representation-level monitoring of factual integrity during model updates.
papers.key_findings:
Poisoning shifts probability mass from correct to counterfactual answers without increasing ambiguity, indicating systematic belief replacement rather than diffuse uncertainty.
Belief flips occur abruptly across checkpoints and are concentrated in late transformer layers (e.g., Layers 29–36 in 3B models).
Activation patching in late layers can partially reverse the corruption, rescuing up to 56.8% of poisoned beliefs.
Poisoned beliefs generalize beyond training prompts, selectively degrading commonsense reasoning (HellaSwag) while leaving alignment benchmarks (TruthfulQA, HH-RLHF) largely stable.
Cross-lingual transfer of poisoned beliefs is imperfect, with weaker expression and higher ambiguity in languages not used during poisoning (e.g., Russian vs. English).
papers.abstract: We show that continual pretraining on plausible misinformation can overwrite specific factual knowledge in large language models without degrading overall performance. Unlike prior poisoning work under static pretraining, we study repeated exposure to counterfactual claims during continual updates. Using paired fact-counterfact items with graded poisoning ratios, we track how internal preferences between competing facts evolve across checkpoints, layers, and model scales. Even moderate poisoning (50-100%) flips over 55% of responses from correct to counterfactual while leaving ambiguity nearly unchanged. These belief flips emerge abruptly, concentrate in late layers (e.g., Layers 29-36 in 3B models), and are partially reversible via patching (up to 56.8%). The corrupted beliefs generalize beyond poisoned prompts, selectively degrading commonsense reasoning while leaving alignment benchmarks largely intact and transferring imperfectly across languages. These results expose a failure mode of continual pre-training in which targeted misinformation replaces internal factual representations without triggering broad performance collapse, motivating representation-level monitoring of factual integrity during model updates.

papers.title: Uncertainty Unveiled: Can Exposure to More In-context Examples Mitigate Uncertainty for Large Language Models?
papers.research_question: How does increasing the number of in-context examples influence the predictive uncertainty of large language models in in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Additional in-context examples reduce total uncertainty in LLMs by injecting task-specific knowledge, which primarily diminishes epistemic uncertainty and enhances performance.
papers.conclusion: Additional examples reduce uncertainty by integrating task-specific knowledge, primarily through reducing epistemic uncertainty, and many-shot ICL increases model confidence by reallocating logit mass and enlarging the logit margin.
papers.key_findings:
Additional in-context examples reduce total uncertainty (TU) in both simple and complex tasks.
The reduction in TU is primarily driven by a decrease in epistemic uncertainty (EU).
For complex tasks, the benefits of many-shot ICL only emerge after addressing the increased noise and uncertainty from longer inputs.
Many-shot ICL enables LLMs to concentrate more logit mass on the correct answer and amplify the disparity between correct and incorrect options.
The quality of uncertainty measures (as indicated by AUROC) remains high across different shot counts.
papers.limitation:
Exclusion of open-ended tasks such as summarization and translation due to lack of robust uncertainty quantification techniques.
Limited exploration of other ICL paradigms like unsupervised ICL, reinforced ICL, and chain-of-thought prompting.
future_direction: Applying uncertainty quantification methodologies to open-ended generative tasks.
Extending uncertainty analysis to reasoning-intensive contexts like chain-of-thought prompting.
Broadening the applicability of ICL in high-stakes domains.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in handling long sequences have facilitated the exploration of long-context in-context learning (ICL). While much of the existing research emphasizes performance improvements driven by additional in-context examples, the influence on the trustworthiness of generated responses remains underexplored. This paper addresses this gap by investigating how increased examples influence predictive uncertainty, an essential aspect in trustworthiness. We begin by systematically quantifying the uncertainty of ICL with varying shot counts, analyzing the impact of example quantity. Through uncertainty decomposition, we introduce a novel perspective on performance enhancement, with a focus on epistemic uncertainty (EU). Our results reveal that additional examples reduce total uncertainty in both simple and complex tasks by injecting task-specific knowledge, thereby diminishing EU and enhancing performance. For complex tasks, these advantages emerge only after addressing the increased noise and uncertainty associated with longer inputs. Finally, we explore the evolution of internal confidence across layers, unveiling the mechanisms driving the reduction in uncertainty.

papers.title: When Truth Is Overridden: Uncovering the Internal Origins of Sycophancy in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does sycophantic behavior arise within the internal mechanisms of Large Language Models?
papers.core_contribution: Sycophancy in LLMs arises from a two-stage process in late layers: a preference shift towards the user's opinion and a deeper representational divergence, while user expertise claims are not internally encoded and thus have minimal impact.
papers.conclusion: Sycophancy is not a surface-level artifact but emerges from a structural override of learned knowledge in deeper layers, with implications for alignment and truthful AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
User opinions strongly induce sycophancy, while expertise framing has minimal impact.
Sycophancy emerges in two stages: a late-layer output preference shift and a deeper representational divergence.
Activation patching confirms the causal role of late-layer representations in sycophantic behavior.
Expertise levels are not encoded internally, as their representations overlap, unlike opinion prompts which form distinct clusters.
First-person prompts induce higher sycophancy than third-person prompts due to stronger representational perturbations in deeper layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often exhibit sycophantic behavior, agreeing with user-stated opinions even when those contradict factual knowledge. While prior work has documented this tendency, the internal mechanisms that enable such behavior remain poorly understood. In this paper, we provide a mechanistic account of how sycophancy arises within LLMs. We first systematically study how user opinions induce sycophancy across different model families. We find that simple opinion statements reliably induce sycophancy, whereas user expertise framing has a negligible impact. Through logit-lens analysis and causal activation patching, we identify a two-stage emergence of sycophancy: (1) a late-layer output preference shift and (2) deeper representational divergence. We also verify that user authority fails to influence behavior because models do not encode it internally. In addition, we examine how grammatical perspective affects sycophantic behavior, finding that first-person prompts (``I believe...'') consistently induce higher sycophancy rates than third-person framings (``They believe...'') by creating stronger representational perturbations in deeper layers. These findings highlight that sycophancy is not a surface-level artifact but emerges from a structural override of learned knowledge in deeper layers, with implications for alignment and truthful AI systems.

papers.title: Confidence Regulation Neurons in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models represent and regulate uncertainty in next-token predictions? Specifically, what are the roles of entropy neurons and token frequency neurons in confidence calibration?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and analyzes two types of confidence-regulation neurons in LLMs: entropy neurons, which modulate output entropy via an unembedding null space and LayerNorm, and token frequency neurons, which adjust the output distribution towards or away from the unigram distribution.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess dedicated neurons for confidence regulation, which operate through specific mechanisms such as writing to the unembedding null space and modulating the distance to the unigram distribution, highlighting the importance of these components for calibration.
papers.key_findings:
Entropy neurons write to an effective null space of the unembedding matrix and use the final LayerNorm scale to modulate output entropy with minimal direct effect on logits.
Token frequency neurons boost or suppress token logits proportionally to their frequency, shifting the output distribution towards or away from the unigram distribution.
These neurons act as hedging mechanisms, increasing loss on correct predictions but preventing loss spikes on incorrect ones.
Entropy neurons are present across various model families and scales (up to 7B parameters).
In induction tasks, entropy neurons increase output entropy to decrease confidence when repeating subsequences.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to decoder-only Transformer-based language models.
Token frequency neurons are identified only in models for which the training corpus is known.
The case study focuses solely on induction.
Entropy neurons might be a byproduct of dropout regularization, as all analyzed models were trained with dropout.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to encoder-decoder models.
Study other potential confidence-regulation mechanisms.
Investigate the role of dropout in the formation of entropy neurons.
Explore interactions between confidence-regulation neurons and other model components.
papers.abstract: Despite their widespread use, the mechanisms by which large language models (LLMs) represent and regulate uncertainty in next-token predictions remain largely unexplored. This study investigates two critical components believed to influence this uncertainty: the recently discovered entropy neurons and a new set of components that we term token frequency neurons. Entropy neurons are characterized by an unusually high weight norm and influence the final layer normalization (LayerNorm) scale to effectively scale down the logits. Our work shows that entropy neurons operate by writing onto an unembedding null space, allowing them to impact the residual stream norm with minimal direct effect on the logits themselves. We observe the presence of entropy neurons across a range of models, up to 7 billion parameters. On the other hand, token frequency neurons, which we discover and describe here for the first time, boost or suppress each token's logit proportionally to its log frequency, thereby shifting the output distribution towards or away from the unigram distribution. Finally, we present a detailed case study where entropy neurons actively manage confidence in the setting of induction, i.e. detecting and continuing repeated subsequences.

papers.title: Do I Know This Entity? Knowledge Awareness and Hallucinations in Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the mechanisms behind hallucinations in language models, specifically regarding entity recognition and knowledge awareness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers entity recognition directions in the representation space that encode knowledge awareness and shows they causally affect knowledge refusal and hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models have internal representations of knowledge awareness that affect refusal and hallucinations, and that chat fine-tuning repurposes this existing mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders uncover directions in the representation space that detect whether the model recognizes an entity as known or unknown.
These entity recognition directions generalize across diverse entity types (players, movies, cities, songs).
The directions causally affect knowledge refusal: steering can induce the model to refuse on known entities or hallucinate on unknown entities.
The directions disrupt the attention of downstream heads in the factual recall circuit, suppressing attribute extraction.
Early entity recognition directions regulate the model's expression of knowledge uncertainty, and uncertainty directions are predictive of incorrect answers.
papers.limitation: The methodology for labeling entities as known or unknown might introduce inaccuracies, as the model could guess attributes or fail to recall specific attributes while knowing about the entity.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in large language models are a widespread problem, yet the mechanisms behind whether models will hallucinate are poorly understood, limiting our ability to solve this problem. Using sparse autoencoders as an interpretability tool, we discover that a key part of these mechanisms is entity recognition, where the model detects if an entity is one it can recall facts about. Sparse autoencoders uncover meaningful directions in the representation space, these detect whether the model recognizes an entity, e.g. detecting it doesn't know about an athlete or a movie. This suggests that models can have self-knowledge: internal representations about their own capabilities. These directions are causally relevant: capable of steering the model to refuse to answer questions about known entities, or to hallucinate attributes of unknown entities when it would otherwise refuse. We demonstrate that despite the sparse autoencoders being trained on the base model, these directions have a causal effect on the chat model's refusal behavior, suggesting that chat finetuning has repurposed this existing mechanism. Furthermore, we provide an initial exploration into the mechanistic role of these directions in the model, finding that they disrupt the attention of downstream heads that typically move entity attributes to the final token.

papers.title: DYNAMICQA: Tracing Internal Knowledge Conflicts in Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the effect of intra-memory conflict on language models' ability to accept relevant context?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that language models exhibit greater intra-memory conflict with dynamic facts, and these facts are harder to update with context, indicating challenges for retrieval-augmented generation.
papers.conclusion: The study concludes that intra-memory conflict affects context utilization in LMs, and dynamic facts are more difficult to update, highlighting issues for RAG systems.
papers.key_findings:
LMs show higher intra-memory conflict for dynamic facts compared to static facts.
Dynamic facts are harder to update with context, leading to more stubborn instances.
Semantic entropy does not reliably predict persuasion by context.
Temporality has a stronger negative correlation with persuasion than popularity or semantic entropy.
Llama-2 has the highest accuracy and persuasion but also the highest entropy among the models tested.
future_direction: Developing better measures for intra-memory conflict
Exploring other indicators of context use in RAGs
papers.abstract: Knowledge-intensive language understanding tasks require Language Models (LMs) to integrate relevant context, mitigating their inherent weaknesses, such as incomplete or outdated knowledge. However, conflicting knowledge can be present in the LM's parameters, termed intra-memory conflict, which can affect a model's propensity to accept contextual knowledge. To study the effect of intra-memory conflict on an LM's ability to accept relevant context, we utilize two knowledge conflict measures and a novel dataset containing inherently conflicting data, DynamicQA. This dataset includes facts with a temporal dynamic nature where facts can change over time and disputable dynamic facts, which can change depending on the viewpoint. DynamicQA is the first to include real-world knowledge conflicts and provide context to study the link between the different types of knowledge conflicts. We also evaluate several measures on their ability to reflect the presence of intra-memory conflict: semantic entropy and a novel coherent persuasion score. With our extensive experiments, we verify that LMs exhibit a greater degree of intra-memory conflict with dynamic facts compared to facts that have a single truth value. Furthermore, we reveal that facts with intra-memory conflict are harder to update with context, suggesting that retrieval-augmented generation will struggle with the most commonly adapted facts.

papers.title: How Pre-trained Language Models Capture Factual Knowledge? A Causal-Inspired Analysis
papers.research_question: Which word-level associations (knowledge-dependent, positionally close, highly co-occurred) do Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) depend on to capture factual knowledge, and is this dependence effective?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that pre-trained language models capture factual knowledge more by relying on positionally close and highly co-occurred words than knowledge-dependent words, and that this dependence is less effective for factual knowledge capture.
papers.conclusion: PLMs capture factual knowledge ineffectively because they rely more on positionally close and highly co-occurred associations rather than knowledge-dependent associations.
papers.key_findings:
PLMs depend more on positionally close and highly co-occurred associations than the knowledge-dependent association to capture factual knowledge.
Depending on the knowledge-dependent association is more effective for factual knowledge capture than positional close and highly co-occurred associations.
PLMs capture factual knowledge ineffectively because they depend more on ineffective associations.
Dependence on positionally close words leads to overfitting on pre-training samples and poor generalization to unseen queries.
The proposed causal-inspired method can quantify word-level dependence in mask language modeling.
papers.abstract: Recently, there has been a trend to investigate the factual knowledge captured by Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs). Many works show the PLMs' ability to fill in the missing factual words in cloze-style prompts such as "Dante was born in [MASK]." However, it is still a mystery how PLMs generate the results correctly: relying on effective clues or shortcut patterns? We try to answer this question by a causal-inspired analysis that quantitatively measures and evaluates the word-level patterns that PLMs depend on to generate the missing words. We check the words that have three typical associations with the missing words: knowledge-dependent, positionally close, and highly co-occurred. Our analysis shows: (1) PLMs generate the missing factual words more by the positionally close and highly co-occurred words than the knowledge-dependent words; (2) the dependence on the knowledge-dependent words is more effective than the positionally close and highly co-occurred words. Accordingly, we conclude that the PLMs capture the factual knowledge ineffectively because of depending on the inadequate associations.

papers.title: Learning and Unlearning of Fabricated Knowledge in Language Models
papers.research_question: What happens when a new piece of knowledge is introduced into the training data and how long does it last while a large language model (LM) continues to train?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that knowledge-conflicting facts are most enduring in language models and proposes a sparsification method to erase them while preserving task performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper discovers that knowledge-conflicting facts endure for many updates and cause inappropriate priming, and shows that their impact can be mitigated via multi-step sparse updates while preserving main task training.
papers.key_findings:
Facts that conflict with common knowledge are remembered for tens of thousands of training steps, while mundane and scrambled facts are forgotten more rapidly.
Knowledge-conflicting facts can prime how the model hallucinates on logically unrelated prompts.
There is a sweet spot in fact novelty (between consistency and randomness) for memory durability.
The impact of knowledge-conflicting facts can be erased by multi-step sparse updates while preserving task performance.
future_direction: Extend the Outlandish dataset further
papers.abstract: What happens when a new piece of knowledge is introduced into the training data and how long does it last while a large language model (LM) continues to train? We investigate this question by injecting facts into LMs from a new probing dataset, "Outlandish", which is designed to permit the testing of a spectrum of different fact types. When studying how robust these memories are, there appears to be a sweet spot in the spectrum of fact novelty between consistency with world knowledge and total randomness, where the injected memory is the most enduring. Specifically we show that facts that conflict with common knowledge are remembered for tens of thousands of training steps, while prompts not conflicting with common knowledge (mundane), as well as scrambled prompts (randomly jumbled) are both forgotten much more rapidly. Further, knowledge-conflicting facts can "prime'' how the language model hallucinates on logically unrelated prompts, showing their propensity for non-target generalization, while both mundane and randomly jumbled facts prime significantly less. Finally, we show that impacts of knowledge-conflicting facts in LMs, though they can be long lasting, can be largely erased by novel application of multi-step sparse updates, even while the training ability of the model is preserved. As such, this very simple procedure has direct implications for mitigating the effects of data poisoning in training.

papers.title: Facts as Experts: Adaptable and Interpretable Neural Memory over Symbolic Knowledge
papers.research_question: How can we interface a neural language model with an interpretable symbolic memory to make knowledge accessible and modifiable without retraining?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neural language model (Facts-as-Experts) with an explicit interface to a symbolic fact memory, enabling knowledge updates without retraining and improving performance on knowledge-intensive QA tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a method for interfacing a neural language model with a symbolic memory, demonstrating improved QA performance and the ability to modify knowledge without retraining.
papers.key_findings:
FaE outperforms baseline models (FOFE, EmQL, EaE) on FreebaseQA and WebQuestionsSP QA datasets.
FaE can effectively answer questions using new facts injected into its memory at inference time without retraining.
FaE can update stale memories by overwriting facts, though performance decreases when new facts contradict pretraining data.
Removing overlapping entity pairs between pretraining/finetuning and test data reduces performance, indicating some memorization of paraphrases.
FaE shows a zero-shot capability, answering around a quarter of answerable questions without fine-tuning.
papers.limitation: Updating stale memories (where new facts contradict pretraining data) is more difficult and results in a performance drop, indicating the mixing between contextual representations and knowledge requires further research.
future_direction: Addressing the difficulty of updating stale memories and the problem of deleting knowledge.
papers.abstract: Massive language models are the core of modern NLP modeling and have been shown to encode impressive amounts of commonsense and factual information. However, that knowledge exists only within the latent parameters of the model, inaccessible to inspection and interpretation, and even worse, factual information memorized from the training corpora is likely to become stale as the world changes. Knowledge stored as parameters will also inevitably exhibit all of the biases inherent in the source materials. To address these problems, we develop a neural language model that includes an explicit interface between symbolically interpretable factual information and subsymbolic neural knowledge. We show that this model dramatically improves performance on two knowledge-intensive question-answering tasks. More interestingly, the model can be updated without re-training by manipulating its symbolic representations. In particular this model allows us to add new facts and overwrite existing ones in ways that are not possible for earlier models.

papers.title: Information Anxiety in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the effect of entity popularity on the internal reasoning and retrieval mechanisms of LLMs, and do queries about popular entities cause ambiguity or confusion?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces 'information anxiety', a phenomenon where LLMs exhibit internal strains when processing highly popular queries, leading to rapid convergence of probability distributions but poor attention and inconsistent fact retrieval across lexical variations.
papers.conclusion: Information anxiety reveals vulnerabilities in LLMs' processing of prevalent information, emphasizing the need for robust evaluation and better pretraining data scrutiny.
papers.key_findings:
For highly popular questions, the predicted probability distribution converges earlier to the target distribution.
LLMs pay lower attention to constraint tokens in popular queries, indicating poor engagement with query details.
Retrieved facts across lexical variations become more dissimilar as query popularity increases, showing sensitivity to phrasing.
LLMs struggle to segregate facts from distinct relations for popular subjects, leading to higher inter-relation similarity.
Despite internal inconsistencies, LLMs remain confident in predictions for popular queries, as shown by high probability scores.
papers.limitation:
Entity and popularity formatted datasets like PopQA are hard to curate.
Developing better proxies for entity popularity in pretraining data is non-trivial.
Challenges in tracking and standardizing pretraining data quality due to volume and closed-source nature.
future_direction: Reducing sensitivity to lexical variations in knowledge queries.
Reducing popularity-dependent strains in internal mechanisms of LLMs.
Exploring alternative proxies for entity popularity in pretraining corpora.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance as knowledge repositories, enabling models to understand user queries and generate accurate and context-aware responses. Extensive evaluation setups have corroborated the positive correlation between the retrieval capability of LLMs and the frequency of entities in their pretraining corpus. We take the investigation further by conducting a comprehensive analysis of the internal reasoning and retrieval mechanisms of LLMs. Our work focuses on three critical dimensions - the impact of entity popularity, the models' sensitivity to lexical variations in query formulation, and the progression of hidden state representations across LLM layers. Our preliminary findings reveal that popular questions facilitate early convergence of internal states toward the correct answer. However, as the popularity of a query increases, retrieved attributes across lexical variations become increasingly dissimilar and less accurate. Interestingly, we find that LLMs struggle to disentangle facts, grounded in distinct relations, from their parametric memory when dealing with highly popular subjects. Through a case study, we explore these latent strains within LLMs when processing highly popular queries, a phenomenon we term information anxiety. The emergence of information anxiety in LLMs underscores the adversarial injection in the form of linguistic variations and calls for a more holistic evaluation of frequently occurring entities.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
papers.limitation: Layer removal has a more significant negative effect on generative tasks compared to multiple-choice tasks, especially for smaller models.
future_direction: Exploring post-training to restore performance after pruning
Improving model training efficiency by reducing inherent redundancy
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in performance, their size has escalated significantly, with current LLMs containing billions or even trillions of parameters. However, in this study, we discovered that many layers of LLMs exhibit high similarity, and some layers play a negligible role in network functionality. Based on this observation, we define a metric called Block Influence (BI) to gauge the significance of each layer in LLMs. We then propose a straightforward pruning approach: layer removal, in which we directly delete the redundant layers in LLMs based on their BI scores. Experiments demonstrate that our method, which we call ShortGPT, significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in model pruning. Moreover, ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization-like methods, enabling further reduction in parameters and computation. The ability to achieve better results through simple layer removal, as opposed to more complex pruning techniques, suggests a high degree of redundancy in the model architecture.

papers.title: The Shape of Beliefs: Geometry, Dynamics, and Interventions along Representation Manifolds of Language Models' Posteriors
papers.research_question: How are prompt-conditioned beliefs encoded in representation space, how do they update with new evidence, and how can interventions reshape them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that beliefs in LLMs are encoded as curved manifolds in representation space, and that linear steering often fails to preserve the intended belief family, while geometry-aware steering based on linear field probes is more effective.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that rich structure emerges naturally in LLMs and that purely linear concept representations are often an inadequate abstraction, highlighting the importance of geometry-aware methods for interpretability and intervention.
papers.key_findings:
Belief manifolds for distribution parameters (mean and standard deviation) are curved in representation space.
Linear field probes can tile the manifold and decode parameters with high accuracy and smooth variation.
When the input distribution changes, the model updates its beliefs along trajectories on the manifold, with different timescales for mean and variance.
Linear steering can push activations off-manifold, causing coupled shifts in other parameters (e.g., variance).
Geometry-aware steering using linear field probes better preserves the intended belief family and avoids unintended coupled shifts.
papers.limitation:
Relies on small open-source base models and focuses on a restricted family of prompt distributions (time-series), which may not capture the diversity of internal geometries in other settings.
The assumption that beliefs live on manifolds indexable by interpretable parameters may not hold in natural language tasks where latent variables are not fully parameterizable.
Does not investigate causal attribution to uncover which neuronal structure or circuits are responsible for the observed geometry.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) represent prompt-conditioned beliefs (posteriors over answers and claims), but we lack a mechanistic account of how these beliefs are encoded in representation space, how they update with new evidence, and how interventions reshape them. We study a controlled setting in which Llama-3.2 generates samples from a normal distribution by implicitly inferring its parameters (mean and standard deviation) given only samples from the distribution in context. We find representations of curved "belief manifolds" for these parameters form with sufficient in-context learning and study how the model adapts when the distribution suddenly changes. While standard linear steering often pushes the model off-manifold and induces coupled, out-of-distribution shifts, geometry and field-aware steering better preserves the intended belief family. Our work demonstrates an example of linear field probing (LFP) as a simple approach to tile the data manifold and make interventions that respect the underlying geometry. We conclude that rich structure emerges naturally in LLMs and that purely linear concept representations are often an inadequate abstraction.

papers.title: Truth-value judgment in language models: 'truth directions' are context sensitive
papers.research_question: How does context affect the truth-value probes in large language models, and are these probes coherently incorporating contextual information?
papers.core_contribution: Truth-value probes are context sensitive but also sensitive to irrelevant information, and truth-value directions causally mediate natural language inference.
papers.conclusion: Truth-value directions are context sensitive and causally mediate inference, but probes are not fully coherent.
papers.key_findings:
Truth-value probes are sensitive to context, but also to irrelevant information.
The type of errors (consistency errors) depend on the layer, model, and data.
Probes trained without premises (no-prem) still show context sensitivity, indicating that prior beliefs are not represented independently.
Instruction-tuned models show different error patterns (more E4 errors) compared to pretrained-only models.
Truth-value directions causally mediate natural language inference (intervention experiment).
papers.abstract: Recent work has demonstrated that the latent spaces of large language models (LLMs) contain directions predictive of the truth of sentences. Multiple methods recover such directions and build probes that are described as uncovering a model's "knowledge" or "beliefs". We investigate this phenomenon, looking closely at the impact of context on the probes. Our experiments establish where in the LLM the probe's predictions are (most) sensitive to the presence of related sentences, and how to best characterize this kind of sensitivity. We do so by measuring different types of consistency errors that occur after probing an LLM whose inputs consist of hypotheses preceded by (negated) supporting and contradicting sentences. We also perform a causal intervention experiment, investigating whether moving the representation of a premise along these truth-value directions influences the position of an entailed or contradicted sentence along that same direction. We find that the probes we test are generally context sensitive, but that contexts which should not affect the truth often still impact the probe outputs. Our experiments show that the type of errors depend on the layer, the model, and the kind of data. Finally, our results suggest that truth-value directions are causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.

papers.title: Blackbox meets blackbox: Representational Similarity and Stability Analysis of Neural Language Models and Brains
papers.research_question: How sensitive are neural language model representations to prior context, and how do these representations compare to human brain activations during story reading?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Representational Stability Analysis (ReStA) to analyze context-dependence in neural language models, finding that LSTM-based models are more similar to brain representations than transformer-based models, and that deeper layers are more context-dependent.
papers.conclusion: ReStA and RSA are useful for comparing models and brains, but caution is required due to low correlations. LSTM-based models are more similar to brain data, and brain data may only reflect shallow linguistic processing.
papers.key_findings:
LSTM-based models (GoogleLM and ELMO) show higher similarity between their two layers compared to BERT.
For LSTM-based models, the first layer is less sensitive to context length than the last layer, suggesting a hierarchical encoding mechanism.
Transformer-based models (BERT) are more sensitive to context length overall, and their first layer is more context-dependent than the last layer.
Among the models, UniSentEnc learns very different representations from the others, possibly due to different training objectives.
LSTM-based models achieve higher similarity with brain data compared to GloVe and transformer-based models, and their lower layers align better with brain representations.
papers.limitation:
Standard RSA assumes all features of the representational spaces have equal contributions, leading to information loss.
The representational similarity between all models and the brain images remains very low.
Inherent issues in the brain data (e.g., hemodynamic response delay, noise) and complexity of the story reading task make evaluation hard.
future_direction: Perform further analysis on various (bigger) datasets to better interpret what is happening in both the brain and computational models.
Postpone further analysis with the predictive approach (linear regression) to future studies.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we define and apply representational stability analysis (ReStA), an intuitive way of analyzing neural language models. ReStA is a variant of the popular representational similarity analysis (RSA) in cognitive neuroscience. While RSA can be used to compare representations in models, model components, and human brains, ReStA compares instances of the same model, while systematically varying single model parameter. Using ReStA, we study four recent and successful neural language models, and evaluate how sensitive their internal representations are to the amount of prior context. Using RSA, we perform a systematic study of how similar the representational spaces in the first and second (or higher) layers of these models are to each other and to patterns of activation in the human brain. Our results reveal surprisingly strong differences between language models, and give insights into where the deep linguistic processing, that integrates information over multiple sentences, is happening in these models. The combination of ReStA and RSA on models and brains allows us to start addressing the important question of what kind of linguistic processes we can hope to observe in fMRI brain imaging data. In particular, our results suggest that the data on story reading from Wehbe et al. (2014) contains a signal of shallow linguistic processing, but show no evidence on the more interesting deep linguistic processing.

papers.title: How do language models learn facts? Dynamics, curricula and hallucinations
papers.research_question: How do language models acquire factual knowledge during training, and what are the dynamics, the impact of data distribution, and the challenges of integrating new knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a three-phase learning process for factual recall in language models, shows how data distribution affects dynamics, and demonstrates that fine-tuning to add new knowledge is challenging due to hallucinations and corruption of existing memories.
papers.conclusion: The paper emphasizes the importance of data distribution in knowledge acquisition and suggests data scheduling strategies to accelerate training, while highlighting the difficulty of integrating new knowledge post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Language models learn factual recall in three phases: initial language understanding, a performance plateau, and then knowledge emergence.
The plateau phase corresponds to the development of attention-based recall circuits.
Imbalanced data distributions shorten the plateau but can lead to overfitting.
Hallucinations (overconfident predictions on unseen individuals) emerge simultaneously with knowledge acquisition.
Fine-tuning to incorporate new knowledge quickly corrupts existing parametric memories.
papers.limitation: The results do not rule out that other qualitative changes may occur during the plateau phase, and they do not provide any mechanistic insights regarding how models acquire individual-specific knowledge.
future_direction: Further investigation is needed to better understand the precise conditions under which data repetition can effectively reduce time spent on performance plateaus during training.
The data scheduling strategy could be dynamically adjusted based on observed plateau termination.
papers.abstract: Large language models accumulate vast knowledge during pre-training, yet the dynamics governing this acquisition remain poorly understood. This work investigates the learning dynamics of language models on a synthetic factual recall task, uncovering three key findings: First, language models learn in three phases, exhibiting a performance plateau before acquiring precise factual knowledge. Mechanistically, this plateau coincides with the formation of attention-based circuits that support recall. Second, the training data distribution significantly impacts learning dynamics, as imbalanced distributions lead to shorter plateaus. Finally, hallucinations emerge simultaneously with knowledge, and integrating new knowledge into the model through fine-tuning is challenging, as it quickly corrupts its existing parametric memories. Our results emphasize the importance of data distribution in knowledge acquisition and suggest novel data scheduling strategies to accelerate neural network training.

papers.title: Overthinking the Truth: Understanding how Language Models Process False Demonstrations
papers.research_question: Why do language models imitate incorrect demonstrations in their context, and how does this behavior emerge internally?
papers.core_contribution: Language models 'overthink' when given false few-shot demonstrations, and this harmful imitation is caused by specific 'false induction heads' in late layers that attend to and copy incorrect labels from the context.
